title: V. Elders
section: Book I — The History Of A Family
paragraphs: Some of my readers may imagine that my young man was a sickly, rapturous, poorly developed creature—a pale, consumptive dreamer. On the contrary, Alyosha at this time was a well-built, red-cheeked, clear-eyed lad of nineteen, radiant with health. He was very handsome too, graceful, of moderate height, with dark brown hair, a regular, rather long oval face, and wide-set dark gray eyes that shone; he was very thoughtful, and yet, it seemed, very serene. I'll be told, perhaps, that red cheeks aren't incompatible with fanaticism and mysticism, but I'd say Alyosha was more of a realist than almost anyone. Oh, no doubt, in the monastery he fully believed in miracles, but to my mind miracles are never a stumbling block for the realist. It isn't miracles that predispose realists toward belief. A true realist, if he's an unbeliever, will always find the strength and the wherewithal to disbelieve in the miraculous, and if confronted with a miracle as an irrefutable fact, he'd sooner disbelieve his own senses than admit it. And even if he does admit it, he admits it as a fact of nature previously unrecognized by him. In the realist, faith doesn't spring from the miracle—the miracle springs from faith. Once the realist believes, then his very realism obliges him to admit the miraculous as well. The Apostle Thomas said he wouldn't believe until he saw, but once he did see, he said, “My Lord and my God!” Was it the miracle that forced him to believe? Most likely not; he believed solely because he wanted to believe, and quite possibly he fully believed in the depths of his heart even as he said, “I will not believe until I see.”

I'll be told, perhaps, that Alyosha was slow-witted, undeveloped, hadn't finished his studies, and so on. That he didn't finish his studies is true, but to call him stupid or dull would be a real injustice. I'll simply repeat what I've said above. He took up this path only because, at the time, it alone caught his imagination and presented itself to him as the ideal escape for his soul from darkness into light. Add to this that he was, to some degree, a young man of our own most recent era—that is, honest by nature, craving the truth, searching for it, believing in it, wanting to serve it at once with the whole strength of his soul, seeking immediate action, and ready to sacrifice everything, even his own life, for it. Though these young men, unfortunately, fail to understand that sacrificing one's life is, in many cases, the easiest sacrifice of all, and that to give up, say, five or six years of their seething youth to hard, tedious study—if only to multiply tenfold their power to serve the truth and the cause they've set as their goal—such a sacrifice is entirely beyond the strength of many of them. Alyosha's path ran in the opposite direction, but he chose it with the same thirst for swift accomplishment. As soon as he thought seriously about it, he became convinced of the existence of God and of immortality, and at once he said to himself instinctively: “I want to live for immortality, and I'll accept no half measures.” In just the same way, if he'd decided that God and immortality didn't exist, he'd have become an atheist and a socialist on the spot. For socialism isn't merely a question of labor—it's, above all, the question of atheism, the question of the particular shape atheism has taken in our own day, the question of the Tower of Babel built without God, not to reach heaven from earth but to bring heaven down to earth. Alyosha would have found it strange and impossible to go on living as before. It is written: “Give all that thou hast to the poor and follow Me, if thou wouldst be perfect.”

Alyosha said to himself: “I can't give two roubles instead of 'all,' and only go to mass instead of 'following Him.'” Perhaps his childhood memories brought back our monastery, where his mother might have taken him to mass. Perhaps the slanting sunlight and the holy icon to which his poor “crazy” mother had lifted him up still worked on his imagination. Brooding over such things, he may have come to us hoping to find out whether he could sacrifice everything here, or only “two roubles,” and it was in the monastery that he met this elder. I need to digress here to explain what an “elder” is in Russian monasteries, and I'm sorry to say I don't feel very qualified to do so. I'll try, all the same, to give a rough sketch of it in a few words. Authorities on the subject claim that the institution of “elders” is fairly recent, no more than a hundred years old in our monasteries, though in the Orthodox East—especially at Sinai and Athos—it's existed for over a thousand years. It's said to have existed in ancient Russia too, but through the calamities that befell the country—the Tartars, civil war, the break in relations with the East after Constantinople fell—the institution fell into oblivion. It was revived among us toward the end of the last century by one of the great “ascetics,” as they called him, Païssy Velitchkovsky, and his followers. But to this day it survives in only a handful of monasteries, and has at times been treated almost as an unwelcome innovation in Russia. It flourished especially at the famous Kozelski Optin Monastery. When and how it was introduced into our own monastery, I can't say. There had already been three such elders, and Zossima was the last of them. But he was nearly dying of weakness and disease, and there was no one to take his place. This was an important question for our monastery, since it hadn't up to then been distinguished by anything in particular: it had no relics of saints, no wonder-working icons, no glorious traditions, no historic exploits to its name. Its fame across all of Russia had come through its elders, whom pilgrims flocked for thousands of miles to see and hear.

What, then, was such an elder? An elder was someone who took your soul, your will, into his own soul and his own will. When you chose an elder, you renounced your own will and handed it over to him in complete submission, complete self-abnegation. This novitiate, this harsh school of self-denial, was taken on voluntarily, in the hope of self-conquest, of self-mastery, so that after a lifetime of obedience one might attain perfect freedom—that is, freedom from the self—and escape the fate of those who go through their whole lives without ever finding their true selves within themselves. This institution of elders wasn't founded on theory, but grew out of a thousand years of practice in the East. The obligations owed to an elder aren't the same as the ordinary “obedience” that has always existed in our Russian monasteries. This obligation involves confession to the elder by everyone who has submitted to him, and an unbreakable bond between him and them.

There's a story told, for instance, of the early days of Christianity: one such novice, having failed to carry out some command his elder had laid on him, left his monastery in Syria and went off to Egypt. There, after great feats of asceticism, he was found worthy at last to be tortured and put to death for the faith. When the Church, regarding him as a saint, came to bury him, suddenly, at the deacon's exhortation of “Depart, all ye unbaptized,” the coffin holding the martyr's body left its place and was cast out of the church—and this happened three times. Only at last did they learn that this holy man had broken his vow of obedience and abandoned his elder, and so could not be forgiven, in spite of his great deeds, without the elder's absolution. Only after that could the burial take place. This, of course, is only an old legend. But here's a more recent instance.

A monk was suddenly ordered by his elder to leave Athos, which he loved as a sacred place, a haven of refuge, and to go first to Jerusalem to pay homage to the Holy Places, and then north to Siberia: “There is the place for thee, and not here.” The monk, overwhelmed with grief, went to the Œcumenical Patriarch in Constantinople and begged to be released from his vow of obedience. But the Patriarch answered that not only was he himself unable to release him, but there wasn't, and couldn't be, any power on earth that could release him, except the elder who had laid that duty on him in the first place. In this way, elders are endowed, in certain cases, with unlimited and inexplicable authority. That's why, in many of our monasteries, the institution was at first resisted, almost to the point of persecution. Meanwhile, the elders quickly came to be held in the highest regard among ordinary people. Crowds of the uneducated poor, as well as men of distinction, flocked, for instance, to the elders of our monastery, to confess their doubts, their sins, their sufferings, and to ask for counsel and guidance. Seeing this, opponents of the elders declared that the sacrament of confession was being carelessly and frivolously cheapened, though the constant opening of the heart to the elder, by monk or layman alike, had nothing whatever of the character of the sacrament about it. In the end, however, the institution of elders held on and is becoming established in Russian monasteries. It's true, perhaps, that this instrument—tested over a thousand years for the moral regeneration of a man, carrying him from slavery into freedom and toward moral perfection—can be a double-edged weapon, and may lead some not toward humility and complete self-mastery, but toward the most Satanic pride—that is, toward bondage rather than freedom.

The elder Zossima was sixty-five. He came from a family of landowners, had served in the army in his early youth, and served as an officer in the Caucasus. He must have impressed Alyosha with some particular quality of his soul. Alyosha lived in the elder's cell, and the elder, who was very fond of him, let him wait on him. It should be noted that Alyosha was bound by no formal obligation, and could go wherever he pleased, and be away for whole days at a time. Though he wore the monastic habit, he did so voluntarily, simply so as not to stand apart from the others. No doubt he liked doing it. Possibly his young imagination was deeply stirred by the power and fame of his elder. It was said that so many people had, over the years, come to confess their sins to Father Zossima, and to beg him for words of advice and healing, that he'd developed an almost uncanny intuition, and could tell, from an unfamiliar face alone, what a newcomer wanted and what was weighing on his conscience. He sometimes astonished, even frightened, his visitors by knowing their secrets before they'd said a word.

Alyosha noticed that many—almost all—went in to the elder the first time with apprehension and unease, but came out with bright, happy faces. Alyosha was particularly struck by the fact that Father Zossima wasn't at all severe. On the contrary, he was almost always cheerful. The monks used to say he was drawn more strongly to those who were more sinful, and that the greater the sinner, the more he loved him. There were, no doubt, some among the monks, right up to the end of his life, who hated and envied him, but they were few, and they kept silent, though among them were men of considerable standing in the monastery—one, for instance, among the older monks, noted for his strict fasting and his vows of silence. But the majority stood with Father Zossima, and a great many of them loved him with all their hearts, warmly and sincerely. Some were almost fanatically devoted to him, and would say, though not quite aloud, that he was a saint—no question about it—and, seeing that his end was drawing near, they looked forward to miracles and great glory for the monastery in the near future, once his relics were there. Alyosha had unquestioning faith in the elder's miraculous power, just as he had unquestioning faith in the story of the coffin that flew out of the church. He watched many people come with sick children or relatives, begging the elder to lay hands on them and pray over them, and return shortly after—some the very next day—falling in tears at the elder's feet, thanking him for healing their sick.

Whether they'd really been healed, or had simply improved in the natural course of their illness, was a question that didn't exist for Alyosha, since he fully believed in his teacher's spiritual power, and rejoiced in his fame, in his glory, as though it were his own triumph. His heart pounded, and he practically glowed all over, when the elder came out to the gates of the hermitage into the crowd of waiting pilgrims—humble folk who'd flocked from every corner of Russia to see the elder and get his blessing. They fell down before him, wept, kissed his feet, kissed the ground he stood on, and wailed, while the women held up their children to him and brought him the sick, the “possessed by devils.” The elder spoke to them, read a short prayer over them, blessed them, and sent them on their way. Lately he'd grown so weak, from repeated bouts of illness, that he sometimes couldn't even leave his cell, and pilgrims would wait several days for him to come out. Alyosha didn't wonder why they loved him so, why they fell down before him and wept for the sheer emotion of seeing his face. He understood perfectly well that, for the humble soul of the Russian peasant, worn out by grief and toil, and even more by the endless injustice and endless sin—his own and the world's—it was the greatest need and comfort of all to find someone, something, holy, to fall down before and worship.

“Among us there's sin, injustice, temptation—but still, somewhere on earth there's someone holy and exalted. He has the truth; he knows the truth; so it isn't dead here on earth; so one day it will come to us too, and rule the whole earth, as promised.”

Alyosha knew this was exactly how the people felt—even reasoned. He understood it, but that the elder Zossima really was this saint, this custodian of God's truth—of that he had no more doubt than the weeping peasant women and the sick mothers holding out their children to the elder. His conviction that after his death the elder would bring extraordinary glory to the monastery was, if anything, stronger in Alyosha than in anyone else there, and lately a kind of deep inner flame of rapture had been burning ever more fiercely in his heart. He wasn't in the least troubled that this elder stood before him as a solitary example.

“No matter. He is holy. He carries in his heart the secret of renewal for everyone—that power which will, at last, establish truth on the earth, and then all men will be holy and love one another, and there'll be no more rich or poor, no exalted and no humbled, but all will be as children of God, and the true Kingdom of Christ will come.” That was the dream living in Alyosha's heart.

The arrival of his two brothers, whom he hadn't known before, seemed to make a deep impression on Alyosha. He made friends more quickly with his half-brother Dmitri (even though he arrived later) than with his own full brother Ivan. He was intensely interested in his brother Ivan, but even after Ivan had been in town two months, though they met fairly often, they still weren't close. Alyosha was naturally quiet, and seemed to be waiting for something, embarrassed about something, while his brother Ivan—though Alyosha noticed early on that Ivan looked at him for a long time, curiously—seemed soon to have stopped thinking about him at all. Alyosha noticed it with a certain awkwardness. At first he put his brother's indifference down to the gap in their ages and education. But he also wondered whether Ivan's lack of curiosity and warmth might stem from some other cause entirely unknown to him. He kept imagining that Ivan was absorbed in something—something inward, something important—that he was striving toward some goal, perhaps a very hard one to reach, and that this was why he had no thought to spare for him. Alyosha wondered, too, whether the learned atheist might not feel some contempt for him—a foolish novice. He knew for certain his brother was an atheist. He couldn't take offense at this possible contempt, and yet, with an uneasy embarrassment he couldn't quite explain to himself, he waited for his brother to draw closer to him. Dmitri always spoke of Ivan with the deepest respect, and with a peculiar earnestness. From him, Alyosha learned all the details of the important business that had lately created such a close, remarkable bond between the two elder brothers. Dmitri's enthusiastic remarks about Ivan struck Alyosha all the more since Dmitri was, next to Ivan, almost uneducated, and the two brothers were such a study in contrasts of personality and character that it would be hard to find two men more unlike each other.

It was around this time that the meeting—or rather, the gathering—of this discordant family's members took place in the cell of the elder who had such an extraordinary influence over Alyosha. The pretext for this gathering was a false one. It was at this time that the discord between Dmitri and his father had reached its sharpest point, and their relations had grown unbearably strained. Fyodor Pavlovitch seems to have been the first to suggest, apparently as a joke, that they should all meet in Father Zossima's cell, and that, without appealing directly for his intervention, they might more decently come to some understanding under the elder's conciliating influence. Dmitri, who had never seen the elder, naturally assumed his father was trying to intimidate him, but, secretly blaming himself for his outbursts of temper toward his father on several recent occasions, he accepted the challenge. It should be noted that he wasn't, like Ivan, staying with his father, but living separately at the other end of town. It happened that Pyotr Alexandrovitch Miüsov, who was staying in the district at the time, seized eagerly on the idea. A Liberal of the forties and fifties, a freethinker and an atheist, he may have been driven by boredom, or by the hope of some frivolous diversion. He was suddenly struck with the desire to see the monastery and the holy man for himself. Since his lawsuit with the monastery was still dragging on, he used it as a pretext to see the Superior, hoping to settle it amicably. A visitor coming with such laudable intentions might be received with more attention and consideration than one who came out of mere curiosity. Influence was brought to bear from within the monastery on the elder, who had lately hardly left his cell at all, and had been forced by illness to turn away even his usual visitors. In the end he agreed to see them, and the day was fixed.
“Who made me a judge over them?” was all he said, smiling, to Alyosha.

Alyosha was greatly troubled when he heard about the planned visit. Of that whole quarrelsome, wrangling group, Dmitri was the only one who might take the interview seriously. All the others would come from frivolous motives, ones that might well insult the elder. Alyosha was well aware of that. Ivan and Miüsov would come out of curiosity, perhaps of the crudest kind, while his father might well be planning some piece of buffoonery. Though he said nothing, Alyosha understood his father through and through. The boy, I repeat, was far from as simple as everyone took him for. He awaited the day with a heavy heart. No doubt he kept turning over in his mind how the family discord might be brought to an end. But his chief worry concerned the elder. He trembled for him, for his reputation, and dreaded any affront to him—especially the refined, courteous irony of Miüsov, and the supercilious half-remarks of the highly educated Ivan. He even thought of warning the elder, telling him something about them beforehand, but on second thought said nothing. He only sent word the day before, through a friend, to his brother Dmitri, that he loved him and expected him to keep his promise. Dmitri was puzzled, since he couldn't remember having made any such promise, but he wrote back that he'd do his utmost not to let himself be provoked “by vileness,” though, even though he deeply respected the elder and his brother Ivan, he was convinced the meeting was either a trap set for him or an unworthy farce.
“All the same, I'd rather bite my own tongue out than fail in respect toward the sainted man you hold in such high regard,” he wrote at the end. Alyosha found little comfort in the letter.
